outputs.L1:
EL CALABOZ, Texas (CNN) -- Eloisa Tamez says she is no longer afraid—only resolute. "I am not backing down," she declared. The U.S. government intends to build a border fence similar to existing structures, and approximately 100 landowners are resisting the plan.

Tamez owns three acres of land along the Texas-Mexico border where the Department of Homeland Security hopes to construct the fence. Her property is a remnant of a 12,000-acre land grant bestowed by Spain to her family in 1767, predating the existence of the United States itself. "It is my history. It is my heritage," she said.

This week, the Justice Department initiated legal action against landowners and municipalities who have denied government surveyors access to their property. Tamez anticipates she will soon face a lawsuit, but remains undeterred. Asked how long she intends to fight, she replied simply, "As long as I have to."

Michael Chertoff, Secretary of Homeland Security, insists that the fence's construction will not be halted by opponents such as Tamez. "Can we simply abandon an enterprise because it is a problem for a particular individual?" he told CNN. "I don't think I can accept that." Chertoff has characterized the relinquishing of land for this purpose as a matter of "civic responsibility."

Chertoff maintains that the fence would curb the steady influx of illegal immigrants crossing the border and reduce drug trafficking. He further argues that it would enhance the safety of Border Patrol agents, who have increasingly faced violent confrontations.

The government's plan calls for 700 miles of fencing along the Mexican border, with 370 miles slated for completion by the end of this year. Roughly 70 miles of that fencing is designated for the Rio Grande Valley, pending the government's success in securing the necessary land.

The Rio Grande serves as a natural boundary along this stretch of the border, though in certain areas it narrows enough to be crossed by swimming. Evidence along the riverbanks attests to this practice: discarded piles of underwear mark where swimmers have emerged, changed into dry clothing carried across in plastic bags, and continued on into the United States.

In response, the Border Patrol has intensified its efforts in the Rio Grande Valley, installing additional lighting and motion-detection sensors. A levee constructed along the river now features a dirt road atop it, used by Border Patrol vehicles for surveillance.

Richard Cortez, mayor of the border town of McAllen, Texas, contends that hiring additional Border Patrol agents, deepening the Rio Grande, and clearing its banks of dense vegetation would offer more effective border security than a fence. He derides the proposed structure as "a multibillion-dollar speed bump"—one that would slow, but not halt, illegal immigration. "It is a false sense of security," Cortez said. "America will not be safe. America will continue to waste resources on something that is not going to work."

Cortez and other border mayors opposed to the fence's construction have formed the Texas Border Coalition. The coalition formally requested further consultation with Chertoff regarding the project, but the Department of Homeland Security denied the request this week. While affirming support for continued dialogue with residents and local officials, David Pagan of U.S. Customs and Border Protection wrote in an e-mail, "We do not plan to suspend work on the construction of fence in order to hold a series of additional consultation meetings."

Cortez indicated that his city is considering a legal challenge to the law mandating the fence's construction.

Thus continues the struggle waged by roughly 100 landowners—individuals like Eloisa Tamez—who remain steadfast in their resistance. "I will not allow them to come and survey my land," she said. "I have an American-given right to protect my property."

Eloisa Tamez stands firm on the three acres of land she calls home, land that has belonged to her family for generations along the Texas-Mexico border. Despite mounting pressure from the federal government, Tamez refuses to relinquish her property to make way for a proposed border fence, becoming one of the most visible faces in a growing legal battle that pits private landowners against federal authority.

Tamez is far from alone in her resistance. The Justice Department has moved forward with legal action against approximately 100 landowners and municipalities across the border region, all of whom have similarly denied government surveyors access to assess their properties for the fence's construction. These legal proceedings represent a significant escalation in the government's efforts to secure the land necessary for what officials describe as a critical national security infrastructure project.

For Tamez, however, this dispute transcends simple property rights—it strikes at the heart of her family's identity and history. Her land represents what remains of an extraordinary inheritance: a 12,000-acre Spanish land grant bestowed upon her ancestors in 1767. To Tamez, surrendering this property would mean severing a tangible connection to more than two centuries of family heritage.

On the other side of this conflict stands Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff, who has emerged as a staunch defender of the fence project. Chertoff argues that the barrier serves multiple critical purposes essential to national security. He contends that the fence will significantly reduce illegal immigration across the southern border while simultaneously disrupting drug trafficking operations that exploit vulnerable crossing points. Perhaps most urgently, Chertoff emphasizes the safety concerns facing Border Patrol agents, who have reportedly encountered escalating levels of violence in their daily duties along the border.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Texas landowners fighting the government's plan to build a border fence along the Rio Grande.
counterfactuals.output:
# Landowners Along Rio Grande Fight Federal Government Over Border Fence Plans

**BROWNSVILLE, Texas** — For generations, the Garcia family has farmed the same stretch of land along the Rio Grande, watching the river shift course through South Texas as it has for centuries. Now, they say, the federal government wants to cut their property in half.

"My grandfather worked this land. My father worked this land. And now they're telling me a wall is going to run right through the middle of it," said Elena Garcia, standing near the riverbank on her family's citrus farm outside McAllen. "We won't even be able to reach our own fields without going through a gate that the Border Patrol controls."

The Garcias are among dozens of landowners across the Rio Grande Valley pushing back against federal plans to construct additional border barrier segments along the river, reigniting a legal and political battle that has simmered for more than a decade.

## A Fight Rooted in Geography

Unlike much of the border in Arizona and New Mexico, where a fence can be built directly on the boundary line, the Rio Grande's winding path through Texas creates a unique complication: federal planners typically site the barrier not on the river itself, but on higher ground further inland, to avoid running afoul of an international treaty governing the waterway's flow.

That decision effectively strands thousands of acres of private property — and in some cases, family homes — in a no-man's-land between the fence and the river itself, on the Mexican side of the barrier despite remaining U.S. soil.

"People don't understand — this isn't just about a fence going up on some empty stretch of desert," said Ramiro Trevino, a fourth-generation rancher near Roma. "This is about the government telling me part of my own ranch is going to be on the wrong side of a wall."

## Legal Battles and Eminent Domain

Federal officials have moved to acquire land through eminent domain, filing condemnation lawsuits against landowners who refuse to sell easements or rights of way. Many of these cases remain tied up in federal court, some dating back to construction efforts under previous administrations.

Attorneys representing landowners argue the government has offered inadequate compensation and failed to account for the practical burdens the barrier would impose — from disrupted irrigation systems to blocked access for cattle and equipment.

"These are working farms and ranches, not just abstract parcels of land," said Efren Olivares, an attorney who has represented several Valley families in the disputes. "You can't put a price on three generations of livelihood, and the government's appraisals often don't come close to reflecting what people stand to lose."

The Department of Homeland Security has maintained that border infrastructure remains necessary for security operations, citing drug trafficking and unauthorized crossings in the sector, which has historically seen high volumes of both.

## Local Opposition Crosses Political Lines

The resistance has drawn an unusual coalition of conservative ranchers, environmental groups, and Democratic officials, united less by ideology than by shared frustration over federal authority reaching into private property.

Local environmental organizations warn that construction could damage sensitive habitats along the river, including areas relied upon by endangered ocelots and rare bird species that draw birdwatchers from around the world to the Valley.

"This is prime habitat, and once you fragment it with concrete and steel, you don't get it back," said Marianna Wright, executive director of a wildlife refuge near Alamo, Texas, that has been at the center of past disputes over barrier construction.

Meanwhile, some landowners say they've grown weary of fighting a battle they feel is stacked against them.

"We're not against border security. We understand the concerns," Trevino said. "But nobody up in Washington has to live with a wall running through the middle of what took our family four generations to build."

## What Comes Next

With federal survey crews reportedly already active in parts of the Valley and additional funding earmarked for barrier construction, landowners and their attorneys expect the legal fights to intensify in the coming months.

For families like the Garcias, the outcome will determine not just where a fence stands, but whether the land they've called home for generations remains fully theirs.

"This isn't Washington's land," Garcia said. "It's ours. And we're not going anywhere without a fight."

# Border Fence Dispute: Texas Landowner Challenges Homeland Security Over Property Seizure

**RIO GRANDE VALLEY, Texas** — A legal battle between a South Texas landowner and the Department of Homeland Security has drawn national attention to the human cost of border fence construction, as Eloisa Tamez fights efforts to seize a portion of her family's land through eminent domain.

Tamez, a nursing professor and member of the Lipan Apache tribe, owns a three-acre parcel in El Calaboz that has remained in her family for generations, dating back to a Spanish land grant. The property sits directly in the path of a planned border security fence, prompting DHS to pursue condemnation proceedings after negotiations for access reportedly stalled.

"This land is not just property to me — it is my heritage, my history, and my identity," Tamez said in a statement to supporters. "The government wants to bisect my land and cut off my family from that history without adequate consultation or fair compensation discussions."

Tamez has resisted signing agreements granting DHS immediate access to survey and construct on her land, arguing that the government sidestepped meaningful negotiation and failed to consider alternatives to a full fence structure through residential and agricultural areas.

## Homeland Security's Position

Then-Secretary of Homeland Security Michael Chertoff defended the department's approach, citing security imperatives along the southern border.

"We have a responsibility to secure this nation's borders, and that requires infrastructure in areas that are vulnerable to illegal crossings and smuggling," Chertoff said in remarks addressing the broader fence controversy. "We have made every effort to work with landowners, but where negotiations are not fruitful, the law provides mechanisms for the government to proceed. Border security cannot be held hostage indefinitely to individual property negotiations."

Chertoff has maintained that DHS attempted good-faith outreach to affected landowners, though critics argue the timelines imposed left little room for genuine negotiation.

## Local Officials Voice Concerns

Local elected officials in the Rio Grande Valley have been vocal critics of the fence project, arguing it damages community relationships and disregards the concerns of longtime residents.

Brownsville Mayor Pat Ahumada has been among the most outspoken opponents. "This isn't just about one piece of land — it's about how the federal government is treating an entire region," Ahumada said. "We are talking about families who have lived here for generations, and they're being told to simply hand over their property. That's not how this is supposed to work in America."

Other regional mayors have echoed similar sentiments, emphasizing that the fence would cut through private lands, nature preserves, and historic communities while doing little, in their view, to meaningfully address border security challenges.

"The border fence divides communities that have coexisted along this river for centuries," said one South Texas mayor whose jurisdiction faces similar condemnation actions. "We understand the need for security, but this approach tramples on the rights of the very citizens the government is supposed to protect."

## Legal and Political Context

Tamez's case is one of dozens of eminent domain proceedings initiated under the Secure Fence Act of 2006, which authorized construction of hundreds of miles of barriers along the U.S.-Mexico border. Landowners across Texas have challenged the government's authority to seize land quickly, arguing that DHS's use of expedited legal procedures denies them adequate due process.

Legal advocates supporting Tamez contend that the case highlights broader questions about federal power, indigenous land rights, and the balance between national security policy and individual property rights.

The case remains before federal courts, with Tamez's legal team pursuing arguments centered on due process violations and inadequate compensation offers. Meanwhile, construction on other segments of the border fence has continued in areas where agreements have been reached or condemnation proceedings concluded.

As the litigation continues, Tamez has become a symbol for landowners across the border region grappling with the tension between federal security mandates and long-standing property and cultural ties to the land.

*This report will be updated as developments occur.*

# Border Wall Construction Divides Rio Grande Valley Communities

**MISSION, Texas** — For generations, the Alvarez family has farmed citrus groves along the Rio Grande, their land tracing the river's curves through three generations of ownership. Now, that same land sits at the center of a bitter standoff between local landowners and federal immigration authorities over plans to extend border wall construction through the Rio Grande Valley.

## A Community Divided

The proposed wall segments would cut through private property, wildlife refuges, and historic sites throughout Hidalgo, Cameron, and Starr counties—some of the most ecologically diverse and economically vital land along the entire southern border.

"This isn't just dirt to us," says Maria Alvarez, whose family has farmed here since the 1940s. "The Department of Homeland Security wants to build a 30-foot wall through the middle of our property, cutting us off from nearly 40 acres of our own land."

Local opposition has coalesced around several key concerns: the use of eminent domain to seize private property, environmental damage to sensitive habitats including the National Butterfly Center and Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, and skepticism about whether a wall addresses the region's actual security needs.

## The Federal Position

DHS officials maintain that additional barriers are necessary components of broader border security strategy. In statements to local media, agency representatives have emphasized that construction follows established legal procedures, including required compensation for property acquired through eminent domain proceedings.

"Border barriers in strategic locations remain a critical tool for impeding and denying illegal crossings," a DHS spokesperson stated, echoing language used in previous administrations' justifications for similar projects.

## Legal Battlegrounds

The conflict has increasingly moved into federal courtrooms. Property owners, represented by organizations including the Texas Civil Rights Project, have challenged both the compensation offered for seized land and the environmental review processes—or lack thereof—preceding construction.

Nayda Alvarez (no relation to Maria), another local landowner, describes receiving federal notices with compressed timelines: "They gave us weeks to respond to filings that could take away land my family has owned for generations. The legal process feels stacked against ordinary people."

Environmental groups have separately sued over waived environmental protections, citing authority granted to DHS under the REAL ID Act of 2005, which allows the agency to bypass dozens of environmental and cultural preservation laws in the name of border security.

## Economic and Ecological Stakes

The Rio Grande Valley's unique subtropical ecosystem supports rare species found nowhere else in the United States, drawing bird-watchers and ecotourists whose spending supports local economies. The National Butterfly Center alone has documented over 240 butterfly species.

"We're not just talking about abstract environmental concerns," says a wildlife refuge manager who requested anonymity due to the sensitivity of ongoing litigation. "Wall construction has already required bulldozing habitat, disrupting wildlife corridors that connect ecosystems on both sides of the river."

Local business owners express mixed views. Some cite the wall as unnecessary disruption to a border region that functions as an integrated economic zone with Mexican sister cities like Reynosa and Matamoros. Others believe increased security infrastructure could benefit safety and property values.

## Uncertain Path Forward

As litigation continues, construction has proceeded in fits and starts, with some segments completed while others remain tied up in legal challenges. Community meetings, once sparsely attended, now draw dozens of residents seeking updates on cases affecting their properties.

For families like the Alvarezes, the dispute represents more than policy debate—it's an existential question about their relationship to land that predates the international boundary itself.

# Border Fence Project Faces Mounting Opposition from Texas Landowners, Local Officials

*McALLEN, Texas* — A coalition of landowners, environmental groups, and local officials is intensifying their pushback against federal plans to construct additional border wall segments along the Texas-Mexico border, raising concerns about property rights, environmental damage, and the fence's actual effectiveness in curbing illegal crossings.

McAllen Mayor Richard Cortez has emerged as one of the most vocal critics of the project, arguing that the barrier would do little to address the root causes of migration while causing significant harm to the Rio Grande Valley's economy and ecosystem.

"We've said all along that a wall is not the answer," Cortez said in a recent statement. "This is a 21st-century problem, and we're trying to solve it with a solution from the Middle Ages."

Cortez, who has led the border city through previous rounds of fence construction, noted that much of the private land along the river has already been divided by barriers built during the Bush and Obama administrations, cutting off property owners from their own land — sometimes leaving fields, homes, and even wildlife refuges stranded on the "Mexico side" of the fence.

## Landowners Push Back

For property owners like Nayda Alvarez, whose family has lived along the river for generations, the fight is deeply personal. Alvarez's home sits just south of levee-based fencing constructed years ago, effectively placing her property in a no-man's-land between the barrier and the international boundary.

"They're going to put me in a cage," Alvarez told reporters, describing the emotional toll of watching federal surveyors mark her land for potential seizure. "This is my home. This is where I raised my kids."

Attorneys representing landowners in the Rio Grande Valley say the federal government has moved to use eminent domain to seize private property for construction, often offering compensation that owners say falls far short of fair market value. Legal battles over land condemnation from the last major wave of fence-building remain unresolved in some cases, years later.

"These are multigenerational family farms and ranches," said one attorney representing several affected families. "The government comes in, offers a lowball figure, and if you don't take it, they take you to court. It's an incredibly stressful and often financially devastating process for these families."

## Environmental Concerns

Conservation groups have also raised alarms about the project's impact on protected wildlife areas, including the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge and the National Butterfly Center, both of which lie in the path of proposed construction.

"This isn't just about politics — this is one of the most biodiverse regions in the country," said a spokesperson for a regional conservation nonprofit. "Segmenting these habitats with concrete and steel could have irreversible consequences for endangered species."

## Federal Officials Defend the Project

Despite local opposition, officials from the Department of Homeland Security have maintained that additional barriers are a necessary tool for border security, citing statistics on illegal crossings and drug trafficking in the sector.

"Physical barriers, combined with technology and personnel, are a critical component of a layered border security strategy," a DHS spokesperson said in a written statement, adding that the agency works to "minimize impacts to private landowners" throughout the acquisition process.

Federal officials have pointed to sections of existing fencing as evidence of reduced crossing attempts in certain areas, though independent analysts note that migration patterns are influenced by numerous factors, including economic conditions and enforcement elsewhere along the border.

## A Community Caught in the Middle

For many in the Rio Grande Valley, the debate over the wall has become less about national politics and more about daily life in a region that has long depended on cross-border trade and tourism with neighboring Reynosa, Mexico.

Local business leaders warn that renewed construction could further strain the local economy, discouraging visitors and complicating the seasonal agricultural work that many farms rely on.

Mayor Cortez has called for renewed dialogue between federal officials and the communities most affected by the project, urging Washington to consider alternatives such as increased technology, personnel, and infrastructure investment rather than additional physical barriers.

"We are not against border security," Cortez said. "We are against a wall that divides our community, hurts our economy, and takes people's homes and land without truly making us safer."

As litigation over land seizures continues and construction plans move forward in select areas, the fight over the border fence appears far from over — with landowners, officials, and advocacy groups vowing to continue challenging the project in both the courts and the court of public opinion.

# Border Fence Plans Meet Fierce Resistance from Texas Landowners

**A federal push to extend hundreds of miles of border fencing along the U.S.-Mexico boundary has run headlong into opposition from Texas property owners, setting up legal and political battles that highlight the human cost of national security policy.**

Among the most vocal opponents is Eloisa Tamez, a nursing professor and member of the Lipan Apache tribe, whose family has held land along the Rio Grande in El Calaboz, Texas, for generations—land granted to her ancestors by the King of Spain centuries ago. Tamez has refused to sign documents granting the Department of Homeland Security access to survey her property for fence construction, arguing that the barrier would cut through her land, separating her from the river and effectively ceding U.S. territory to a no-man's-land between the fence and the border itself.

"This is my land," Tamez has said in previous public statements defending her stand. "They want to build a wall through my backyard, and I'm supposed to just accept that?"

Tamez is far from alone. Dozens of landowners, farmers, and local officials across the Rio Grande Valley have voiced similar objections, arguing that the fence would damage property values, disrupt agricultural operations, harm wildlife habitats, and fracture communities that have existed along both sides of the river for generations. Some border towns rely on cross-border commerce and family ties that predate the international boundary itself.

Local governments have joined the pushback. Several Texas counties and cities have passed resolutions opposing the fence, while environmental groups have raised concerns about the barrier's impact on fragile ecosystems, including habitats for endangered species.

## Federal Government Presses Forward

Despite the resistance, Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff has remained firm in defending the fence-building initiative, which stems from the Secure Fence Act of 2006. Chertoff has argued that the fencing is a critical tool for curbing illegal immigration and drug trafficking, and has emphasized that DHS is required by law to move forward with construction.

When landowners have refused access for surveys, the federal government has turned to the courts, filing lawsuits to obtain the right of entry needed to build the fence. Chertoff has also been granted broad authority under REAL ID Act provisions to waive environmental and other regulations that might otherwise slow construction—a power he has invoked to keep the project on schedule.

Chertoff has framed the fence as a necessary, if imperfect, response to what he describes as a porous border that undermines national security and the rule of law. "We're not going to let this be delayed indefinitely," he has said in addressing congressional and public concerns, signaling that legal challenges from landowners would not derail the administration's timeline.

## A Broader Conflict

The standoff in Texas reflects a broader tension playing out across the southern border: the federal government's mandate to secure the boundary versus the rights and livelihoods of those who live along it. Legal experts note that eminent domain gives the government substantial power to acquire land for public use, provided landowners are compensated—but the process has left many in the Rio Grande Valley feeling like an afterthought in a policy debate playing out far from their front doors.

For Tamez and others like her, the fight is about more than property lines. It's a question of sovereignty, heritage, and whether the promise of due process holds up against the machinery of federal border policy.

As court dates loom and construction crews prepare to move forward in contested areas, the clash between Washington's security priorities and the rights of individual landowners shows no signs of resolution—leaving families like the Tamezes caught between their ancestral homes and a wall meant to divide two nations.

---
